deep_why: The core problem is predicting how users will engage with false claims on social media. The method rests on a fundamental principle from social science: people treat online interaction like an exchange, weighing what they must invest (time, attention) against what they gain (social approval, information). By modeling each action as reflecting this negotiation between cost and reward in a time sequence, the approach captures why engagement is not random but driven by shifting incentives that evolve as conversations unfold. This principle holds because user behavior on platforms genuinely responds to context and accumulated emotional signals. This lets the system forecast engagement patterns that static models miss, enabling platforms to understand and potentially interrupt how misinformation takes root and spreads.

When models learn continuously from streaming data, they face a dilemma: either they remember everything (wasting computation on redundant examples) or they forget the past (losing patterns they once learned). The method introduces fingerprints—compact summaries of what the model currently knows—and uses these to score each incoming sample for usefulness. The soundness lies in this principle: a sample is worth keeping if it teaches something the fingerprint summary does not already capture. This works because a good fingerprint reflects the model's actual learned state, making the scoring genuinely informative. By filtering data this way while retaining representative historical examples, the system avoids redundant training while preserving the memory it needs, achieving continuous learning without collapse.

Graph anomaly detection must work across different domains without seeing labeled anomalies, a nearly impossible task if anomalies are too rare to learn from. The approach solves this by extracting normal patterns confidently and then synthetically creating a diverse range of plausible abnormal cases. The principle that makes this sound is this: a good anomaly detector only needs to distinguish what it has learned is normal from anything sufficiently different from that; if the normal pattern is well-captured and synthetic anomalies span the space of deviations, the detector will recognize real anomalies even unseen before. This works because anomalies, by definition, violate the rules of normalcy, and those rules can be inferred from unlabeled data. This strategy scales to new domains without retraining, solving the practical problem of detecting fraud, security threats, and faults in systems where labeled examples are scarce or unavailable.

Auction bidding requires both reasoning (what is my true target value?) and precise action (what bid is best right now?), but large language models reason well yet hallucinate when forced to act. The method splits the task hierarchically: a reasoner module uses language to understand the auction context and strategy, then passes that understanding to an action module tuned for precise bidding. The principle at work is this: reasoning and action benefit from different optimizations, and by decoupling them, each can be refined without corrupting the other. The reasoner grounds the action in prior human knowledge; the action module learns from real auctions. This division of labor works because bidding strategy fundamentally involves both interpretation (understand my goal in context) and execution (pick the right number), and coupling them tight only limits both. The result is a system that bids intelligently in competitive, dynamic markets.

Predicting future events in knowledge bases requires understanding relationships in multiple ways simultaneously—some relationships follow Euclidean logic (distance-based), some express hierarchies (hyperbolic geometry), and some follow logical rules (complex-valued reasoning). The method learns from all three geometries together, with time-aware components capturing how these relationships evolve. The principle at work is this: different mathematical structures capture different kinds of truth, and the richer your representation toolkit, the more complex relational patterns you can detect. By integrating these spaces and updating them dynamically, the model learns representations where each space reinforces the others' blind spots. This works because real knowledge truly does have this layered structure. This richer representation lets systems forecast events in knowledge bases with a depth impossible from any single geometric view alone.

Traffic flow depends on where roads connect (spatial structure) and when congestion happens (temporal patterns), yet standard approaches treat these separately or assume rigid orderings. The method embeds spatial graph structure directly into attention masks so that connected roads can communicate regardless of order, while preserving pre-trained temporal reasoning through selective freezing. The principle underlying this is this: spatial relationships and temporal dynamics are fundamentally intertwined, and by making the attention mechanism aware of the road network's actual topology, the model sees what matters (proximity in the road network) rather than relying on artificial sequence order. This works because traffic genuinely propagates along road connections, and allowing free interaction between spatially adjacent segments lets the model discover real flow patterns. By balancing this new spatial awareness with preserved temporal expertise, the system achieves reliable traffic forecasting in dynamic road networks.

Graph data shifts in two ways: the distribution of node features changes (covariate shift), or the meaning of labels changes (semantic shift). A single detector cannot handle both simultaneously because the features that detect one type often fail on the other. The method learns invariant graph substructures—patterns that remain stable across distribution shifts—by capturing relationships between features and outcomes that hold regardless of what shifted. The principle at work is this: if you identify relationships that survive both types of shift, those relationships are truly causal, not accidental correlation. By learning cross-subgraph patterns that generalize despite shifts, the model builds a robust detector that works on unlabeled data in new domains. This works because real anomalies break genuine rules about how graphs should behave, rules that transcend any single distribution. This unified approach handles the messy real-world scenario where both types of shift occur together.

Once a diffusion model is deployed or fine-tuned by others, the creator loses control over its outputs and cannot prevent unsafe generations. The method adds regulatory layers coupled with special signatures; during sampling, a regulator can inject signals that steer the model away from unsafe outputs at intermediate steps. The principle is this: diffusion iteratively refines noisy data into output; if you monitor and intervene at each step with information the regulator controls, you can redirect the trajectory without retraining. This works because the refinement process is gradual and reversible—intervening mid-process nudges the trajectory without breaking the mathematics of the diffusion itself. By making regulators and model layers tightly coupled, the scheme ensures that the regulator's control persists even after fine-tuning. This solves the urgent problem of governing deployed models that others may misuse.

Zero-knowledge proofs come in two flavors: one uses mathematical setup that is fast but relies on trusted initial conditions; the other requires no setup but is slower and proof size is large. The question is which to use. Empirical measurement on real hardware reveals their true cost-benefit trade-off: setup-based proofs are much faster and compact, but setup-based proofs require trust; transparent proofs are slower and larger but never require trust and resist future quantum computers. The principle that makes this comparison meaningful is this: theoretical complexity only hints at real-world cost; actual code, hardware constraints, and real data matter enormously. By running both systems on actual consumer hardware and profiling bottlenecks, the work shows developers exactly which system fits their constraints and trust model. This lets practitioners make honest decisions between speed and trustlessness.

Mental healthcare experts are scarce, but therapy requires more than just facts—it requires empathy, judgment, and understanding of the person. Small models can be specialized through focused training on clinical examples, augmented with memory of clinical best practices, and guided to reason over each situation step-by-step. The principle at work is this: expertise is learnable if you combine three elements: training on real examples of expert behavior, access to reference knowledge when needed, and structured reasoning about the specific case. Small models are cheaper to run than large ones, so they can be deployed at scale. By measuring alignment to actual therapist behavior through specialized rubrics, the system demonstrates that specialization and guidance can make smaller models expert-like in a narrow, life-critical domain. This creates scalable mental health support.

Fraud hides by mimicking normal transactions across multiple views of the data (account behavior, spending patterns, recipient profiles), and rare frauds get ignored when most training examples are legitimate. The method draws inspiration from how brains detect unusual situations: by monitoring mismatches across different viewpoints and by flagging cases where a transaction deviates from what its neighbors would predict. The principle is this: fraud lives in inconsistency across views and in surprises relative to local norms, and by explicitly measuring both, a detector captures camouflaged deception. This works because fraudsters cannot simultaneously look normal in every dimension; they must cut corners or hide their true intent somewhere. By weighting anomalies more heavily during learning, the system learns to spot the rare cases without being drowned out by the majority. This lets financial platforms catch fraud that traditional methods miss.

User interest is not random noise but a directed journey—people drift toward content they care about as they encounter new information and as their tastes shift over time. The method models this as a directed stochastic process, where user trajectories follow equations that describe both the push (drift) toward meaningful content and the randomness (noise) in choices. The principle at work is this: if you model interest as a continuous process governed by physics-like equations, you can generate smooth, realistic trajectories that capture how taste evolves and why recommendations should change over time. This works because human interest genuinely evolves under forces (what friends share, what algorithms expose, seasonal changes) and chance, and those dynamics are best described by differential equations, not static snapshots. Generating personalized trajectories this way produces recommendations that feel natural and reason about the future of interest, not just its past.

Fake news leaves traces in both images and text: local forgeries (doctored regions) and global anomalies (weird composition or semantics). But these traces only matter if you connect them semantically—knowing what the text says helps you spot whether the image is appropriate. The method extracts and enhances visual features by using semantic information from the text, then fuses all signals by prioritizing modalities based on confidence. The principle is this: forgery cues are strongest when you look across multiple views and let stronger signals guide your attention to weaker ones. By structuring fusion so that high-confidence signals help interpret low-confidence ones, the detector builds a richer picture of whether something is fake. This works because genuine multimedia has coherent semantics across modes, while fakes often mix true and false elements incoherently. By forcing cross-modal semantic alignment, the system catches forgeries that hide in single-modality noise.

When pre-ranking systems mix easy and hard samples indiscriminately, easy samples dominate training (they have low loss) while hard samples—which teach the most—get starved of optimization effort. The method splits them, optimizing easy samples with cheap models and hard samples with powerful ones. The principle is this: not all samples teach equally; hard samples carry disproportionate information, and wasting computation on easy ones wastes the budget for learning. By routing samples intelligently and fitting model strength to difficulty, the system learns faster and reaches higher accuracy with the same compute. This works because optimization converges fastest when you focus computation where it matters most. Adaptive budgeting avoids the inefficiency of uniform scaling, letting recommender systems rank at scale without sacrificing speed or accuracy.

Traditional recommendation systems optimize for immediate clicks, so cold items (new products with unknown click rates) stay hidden in the long tail. The method adds a second objective: predict how exposing a user to a cold item will lead to future organic engagement, using counterfactual logic to estimate long-term growth value. Then it selects which users to show cold items to by balancing instant click value against future growth potential. The principle at work is this: an exposure is most valuable not just if it produces an immediate click but if it plants the seed for sustained future interest. By estimating counterfactual futures—what would have happened if we had not boosted—the system identifies users most likely to generate organic follow-up engagement. This works because real business value comes from lasting user interest, and by optimizing for both short-term and long-term signals, the system cold-starts new products at scale while protecting long-term ecosystem health.
